source_refs.note: Book p. 228: 12.2.8 statement of the Sandwich Theorem and the two sentences leading into 12.2.9

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Sometimes we cannot find a limit by substituting, factorising or dividing. The Sandwich Theorem (also called the Squeeze Theorem) gives another way: trap the difficult function between two easy functions that have the same limit.
Let \(f\), \(g\) and \(h\) be functions such that \(f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x)\) for all numbers \(x\) in some open interval containing "\(c\)", except possibly at \(c\) itself.

If \(\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L\) and \(\lim_{x \to c} h(x) = L\), then
\[\lim_{x \to c} g(x) = L\]

blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text: Many limit problems arise that cannot be directly evaluated by algebraic techniques. They require geometric arguments, so we evaluate an important theorem.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration (not in the book): find \(\lim_{x \to 0} x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x}\).
We cannot substitute \(x = 0\), because \(\sin\frac{1}{x}\) is not defined there and keeps swinging between \(-1\) and \(1\). But \(-1 \le \sin\frac{1}{x} \le 1\), and \(x^{2} \ge 0\), so
\[-x^{2} \le x^{2}\sin\dfrac{1}{x} \le x^{2}\]
Both \(-x^{2}\) and \(x^{2}\) tend to 0 as \(x \to 0\). By the Sandwich Theorem the limit is 0.
The next heading, 12.2.9, uses exactly this theorem to prove the most important trigonometric limit.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. If \(f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x)\) near \(c\) and \(f(x) \to L\), \(h(x) \to L\) as \(x \to c\), then \(g(x) \to L\).
2. The two outer limits must be equal.
3. The inequality is only needed near \(c\), not at \(c\).
4. Use it when algebra fails, especially for functions with \(\sin\) or \(\cos\), which always lie between \(-1\) and \(1\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using two bounds with different limits (for example \(0 \le g(x) \le 1\)): this only tells us the limit, if it exists, is between 0 and 1. It does not give the limit.
2. Writing the inequality the wrong way round, or forgetting that multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it.
3. Writing \(\lim_{x \to 0} x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x} = 0 \cdot \lim_{x \to 0}\sin\frac{1}{x}\): the second limit does not exist, so the product rule cannot be used.
